name: ALIF
say_it: ā — a long open “aa” sound, as in father.
mouth: Mouth open and relaxed. The vowel is carried on the breath; no special tongue contact.
source: For long ā, the sound flows through the open mouth after a fatḥah.
weight: Neutral; its quality follows the surrounding consonants.
avoid: Do not treat bare Alif as an English “uh.” A written hamza (أ / إ) is a separate glottal-stop sound.
notes: Bare Alif commonly lengthens fatḥah to long ā.
Alif does not connect to a following letter on its left.
When hamza appears on or under Alif, pronounce the hamza as a glottal stop.
Example: بَاب has a long ā between the two b sounds.

name: BĀʾ
say_it: b — like the b in boy.
mouth: Close both lips, build a little pressure, then release.
source: Both lips.
avoid: Do not turn it into p; Arabic ب is voiced.
notes: One dot below distinguishes ب from ت and ث.
Bāʾ connects on both sides when neighboring letters allow it.
Its basic sound is b in every position.
Example: بَيْت begins with Bāʾ.

name: TĀʾ
say_it: t — like a clean t in top, with less puff of air than strong English t.
mouth: Touch the tongue tip near the upper front teeth/gum ridge, then release.
source: Tongue tip with the upper front teeth/alveolar area.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as English th or as emphatic ṭ.
notes: Two dots above distinguish ت from ب and ث.
Tāʾ connects on both sides.
Keep it light; ط is the heavy counterpart.
Example: تَمْر begins with Tāʾ.

name: THĀʾ
say_it: th — like the th in think.
mouth: Let the tongue tip touch or slightly pass between the front teeth while air flows.
source: Tongue tip and upper front teeth.
avoid: Do not replace it with s, t, or the voiced th of this.
notes: Three dots above identify ث.
Thāʾ connects on both sides.
The English word think gives a useful approximation.
Example: ثَوْب begins with Thāʾ.

name: JĪM
say_it: j — like the j in jam in standard/Qurʾanic pronunciation.
mouth: Raise the middle of the tongue toward the hard palate and release the voiced sound.
source: Middle of the tongue with the hard palate.
avoid: Do not reduce it to English y or French-style zh.
notes: One dot below distinguishes ج from ح and خ.
Jīm connects on both sides.
In standard Arabic it is taught as the j sound in jam.
Example: جَمَل begins with Jīm.

name: ḤĀʾ
say_it: ḥ — no exact English equivalent; a strong, clear breathy h from the middle throat.
mouth: Keep the mouth open and let air pass through a gently narrowed middle throat.
source: Middle throat (pharyngeal area).
avoid: Do not pronounce it as ordinary ه h, and do not scrape it like خ kh.
notes: Ḥāʾ has no dot.
It shares its basic shape with ج and خ.
The sound is deeper than ه but smoother than خ.
Example: حَقّ begins with Ḥāʾ.

name: KHĀʾ
say_it: kh — like the ch in Scottish loch or German Bach.
mouth: Raise the back of the tongue near the soft palate and let air rub through the narrow space.
source: Upper throat/back of the mouth.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as k, h, or an English “ch.”
notes: One dot above distinguishes خ from ح and ج.
Khāʾ connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: خُبْز begins with Khāʾ.

name: DĀL
say_it: d — like the d in day.
mouth: Touch the tongue tip near the upper front teeth/gum ridge and release with voice.
source: Tongue tip with the upper front teeth/alveolar area.
avoid: Do not turn it into dh; ذ is a different letter.
notes: Dāl has no dot.
It connects to a preceding letter on its right, but not to a following letter on its left.
Its sound stays d in all positions.
Example: دِين begins with Dāl.

name: DHĀL
say_it: dh — like the th in this.
mouth: Place the tongue tip at or slightly between the front teeth and use voice.
source: Tongue tip and upper front teeth.
avoid: Do not replace it with z, d, or the voiceless th of think.
notes: One dot above distinguishes ذ from د.
Dhāl does not connect to a following letter on its left.
The sound matches the voiced th in this.
Example: ذِكْر begins with Dhāl.

name: RĀʾ
say_it: r — a quick tongue tap or light roll, not the English r.
mouth: Tap the tongue tip against the ridge just behind the upper front teeth.
source: Tongue tip and alveolar ridge.
weight: Context-dependent in recitation: sometimes light, sometimes heavy.
avoid: Do not use the English back-of-the-mouth r.
notes: Rāʾ has no dot.
It does not connect to a following letter on its left.
In Qurʾanic recitation its heaviness depends on context.
Example: رَحْمَة begins with Rāʾ.

name: ZĀY
say_it: z — like the z in zoo.
mouth: Bring the tongue close to the front gum ridge and let voiced air pass through.
source: Front of tongue near the alveolar ridge.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as s.
notes: One dot above distinguishes ز from ر.
Zāy does not connect to a following letter on its left.
Its basic sound is z.
Example: زَكَاة begins with Zāy.

name: SĪN
say_it: s — like the s in sun.
mouth: Keep the tongue close to the front teeth/gum ridge and let air hiss through.
source: Front of tongue near the lower incisors and alveolar area.
avoid: Do not voice it as z, and do not make it heavy like ص.
notes: Sīn has no dots and has three “teeth” in its common shape.
It connects on both sides.
Keep the sound light and clear.
Example: سَلَام begins with Sīn.

name: SHĪN
say_it: sh — like the sh in ship.
mouth: Raise the middle/front of the tongue toward the palate while air passes through.
source: Middle of the tongue toward the hard palate.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as s or ch.
notes: Three dots above distinguish ش from س.
Shīn connects on both sides.
Its sound is close to English sh.
Example: شَمْس begins with Shīn.

name: ṢĀD
say_it: ṣ — a heavy/emphatic s; no exact English equivalent.
mouth: Make an s while raising the back of the tongue, giving the sound a fuller, darker quality.
source: Front tongue for s, with the back of the tongue raised.
avoid: Do not flatten it into plain س s.
notes: Ṣād has no dot.
It connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: صَبْر begins with Ṣād.

name: ḌĀD
say_it: ḍ — a heavy Arabic d sound; no exact English equivalent.
mouth: Press one side of the tongue toward the upper molars while keeping the back of the tongue raised.
source: Side of the tongue with the upper molars.
avoid: Do not reduce it to plain د d or ظ ẓ.
notes: One dot above distinguishes ض from ص.
Ḍād connects on both sides.
Its classical articulation uses the side of the tongue against the upper molars.
Example: ضَوْء begins with Ḍād.

name: ṬĀʾ
say_it: ṭ — a heavy/emphatic t; no exact English equivalent.
mouth: Make a t with the tongue tip at the upper gum ridge while raising the back of the tongue.
source: Tongue tip plus a raised back of tongue.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as plain ت t.
notes: Ṭāʾ has no dot.
It connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: طَيِّب begins with Ṭāʾ.

name: ẒĀʾ
say_it: ẓ — a heavy voiced th, made like ذ but with the back of the tongue raised.
mouth: Put the tongue tip at the upper front teeth and add emphatic depth by raising the back of the tongue.
source: Tongue tip and upper teeth, with raised back of tongue.
avoid: Do not replace it with plain ذ dh, ز z, or ض ḍ.
notes: One dot above distinguishes ظ from ط.
Ẓāʾ connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: ظِلّ begins with Ẓāʾ.

name: ʿAYN
say_it: ʿ — no English equivalent; a voiced constricted sound from the middle throat.
mouth: Gently narrow the middle throat and let the voice pass through without closing it completely.
source: Middle throat (pharynx).
avoid: Do not omit it, turn it into a vowel, or replace it with hamza.
notes: ʿAyn has no dot.
It connects on both sides.
The symbol ʿ in transliteration represents this throat sound.
Example: عِلْم begins with ʿAyn.

name: GHAYN
say_it: gh — a voiced friction sound high in the throat/back of the mouth; no exact English equivalent.
mouth: Raise the back of the tongue near the soft palate/uvula and let voiced air rub through.
source: Upper throat/back of the mouth.
avoid: Do not pronounce it as hard English g.
notes: One dot above distinguishes غ from ع.
Ghayn connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: غُرْفَة begins with Ghayn.

name: FĀʾ
say_it: f — like the f in fine.
mouth: Touch the inner lower lip lightly to the upper front teeth and let air pass.
source: Lower lip with upper incisors.
avoid: Do not voice it as v.
notes: One dot above identifies ف in standard Arabic script.
Fāʾ connects on both sides.
Its sound is close to English f.
Example: فَجْر begins with Fāʾ.

name: QĀF
say_it: q — a deep stop made farther back than k; no exact English equivalent.
mouth: Raise the back of the tongue to the uvular/very back palate area, stop the air, then release.
source: Back of the tongue with the uvular/soft-palate area.
avoid: Do not replace it with ك k or English g.
notes: Two dots above distinguish ق from ف.
Qāf connects on both sides.
It is one of the heavy letters in Qurʾanic recitation.
Example: قَلْب begins with Qāf.

name: KĀF
say_it: k — like the k in skin.
mouth: Raise the back of the tongue to the soft palate, briefly stop the air, then release.
source: Back of the tongue with the soft palate.
avoid: Do not make it as deep or heavy as ق q.
notes: Kāf connects on both sides.
Its sound is the ordinary Arabic k.
Compare it with the deeper Qāf ق.
Example: كِتَاب begins with Kāf.

name: LĀM
say_it: l — like a clear/light l.
mouth: Touch the tongue tip/front edge to the gum ridge behind the upper front teeth.
source: Tongue tip/front with the upper alveolar ridge.
weight: Usually light; the l in the name Allāh can be heavy in specific contexts.
avoid: Do not use an overly dark English final-l sound.
notes: Lām connects on both sides.
It is normally pronounced light.
In Allāh, its heaviness depends on the preceding vowel in recitation.
Example: لَيْل begins with Lām.

name: MĪM
say_it: m — like the m in moon.
mouth: Close both lips and let the voiced sound resonate through the nose.
source: Both lips, with nasal resonance.
avoid: Do not leave the lips open; full lip closure is part of m.
notes: Mīm connects on both sides.
It is a nasal consonant.
In tajwīd, some contexts lengthen or conceal its nasal resonance.
Example: مَاء begins with Mīm.

name: NŪN
say_it: n — like the n in noon.
mouth: Touch the tongue tip near the upper gum ridge while voice resonates through the nose.
source: Tongue tip with alveolar ridge, plus nasal resonance.
avoid: Do not turn it into English ng.
notes: One dot above identifies ن.
Nūn connects on both sides.
It carries nasal resonance (ghunnah), especially noticeable in tajwīd rules.
Example: نُور begins with Nūn.

name: HĀʾ
say_it: h — like a clear h in hat.
mouth: Keep the throat open and let breath pass gently without the stronger constriction of ح.
source: Deep throat/open glottal area.
avoid: Do not make it as deep as ح ḥ or rough like خ kh.
notes: Hāʾ connects on both sides.
Its h is lighter than ح.
Its connected forms can look quite different from the isolated form.
Example: هُدَى begins with Hāʾ.

name: WĀW
say_it: w — like w in water; it can also carry the long vowel ū.
mouth: Round the lips for w. For long ū, hold the rounded vowel smoothly.
source: Both lips.
avoid: Do not pronounce consonantal و as v.
notes: Wāw does not connect to a following letter on its left.
As a consonant it sounds w.
After ḍammah, a vowelless و can represent long ū.
Example: وَرْد begins with consonantal Wāw.

name: YĀʾ
say_it: y — like y in yes; it can also carry the long vowel ī.
mouth: Raise the middle of the tongue toward the hard palate without fully blocking the air.
source: Middle of tongue toward the hard palate.
avoid: Do not pronounce consonantal ي as the English long-i sound in my.
notes: Two dots below identify ي in most positions.
Yāʾ connects on both sides.
After kasrah, a vowelless ي can represent long ī.
Example: يَد begins with consonantal Yāʾ.
